title: Dopamine & Prediction Error
content:
Dopamine is not the chemical of pleasure; it is the molecule of anticipation and motivation.

When your brain expects a reward and the outcome is unpredictable (like pulling a slot machine lever or refreshing a social media feed), dopamine spikes significantly higher than if the reward was guaranteed. This is known as a 'Reward Prediction Error.'

Short-form apps and variable feeds hijack this exact circuit: because you never know whether the next swipe will show something boring or exciting, your brain remains in an endless loop of craving and anticipation.
question: What triggers the largest spike of dopamine in the brain?
options: Unpredictable rewards where the outcome is uncertain
Guaranteed outcomes that happen on a fixed schedule

title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
content:
The Sunk Cost Fallacy occurs when you continue an activity, relationship, or bad habit simply because you have already invested time, money, or energy into it—even when quitting is clearly the better choice.

For example, continuing to watch a terrible movie just because you paid for the ticket, or scrolling your phone for another hour because 'the day is already wasted.'

Rational decisions should only be based on future costs and benefits. Past investments are gone forever and cannot be recovered.
question: According to rational decision making, how should past investments (time or money) affect your next choice?
options: They should not influence future choices; only future costs and benefits matter.
You must continue until all past money/time is recovered.
Past investments should always double the priority of the task.
They guarantee that future results will be positive.

title: First-Principles Thinking
content:
First-principles thinking is the practice of boiling a problem down to its most fundamental truths that cannot be deduced any further, and then building up a solution from scratch.

Most people reason by analogy—they copy what others do with slight variations. First-principles thinkers ask: 'What are the basic physical realities of this situation?'

For instance, rather than buying expensive pre-made battery packs, Elon Musk calculated the spot market cost of raw materials (carbon, nickel, aluminum) and built factories to manufacture batteries at 80% lower cost.
question: What is the core step in first-principles thinking?
options: Breaking a problem down to its fundamental, undeniable truths rather than copying existing methods.
Following the consensus of the majority in an industry.
Solving complex equations using financial formulas.
